source: Ormerod and Ross (2024) Modelling insight as a creative domain: process or phenomenology? (MRB 2023 chapter)
finding: PRODIGI (Progress and Detection of Ideas in Generating Insights) keeps progress monitoring and adds a second heuristic, idea discovery, that runs only after impasse. It extends CSP; it does not replace it. Progress monitoring is hill-climbing with a criterion of satisfactory progress, the ratio of work remaining to resources available. Impasse is defined as: no move meets the current criterion.
numbers: Nine-dot criterion = dots left to cancel divided by lines available. About 5% solve the nine-dot in 10 minutes (MacGregor 2001). PRODIGI paper is cited as Ormerod, MacGregor, Banks and Rusconi (2024, under review, unpublished ms).
quote: criterion of satisfactory progress, specified generically as the ratio of work remaining to resources available
limits: A secondary chapter by the same group; the PRODIGI paper itself was not found or read. Not independent. Peer-review status unknown.
agent_relevance: The monitor to build is still the CSP ratio plus an impasse test. What is new is what happens at impasse: look at the properties of past moves and vary them. This matches O4/O5 as a content-specific step, not a generic reset.

source: Ormerod and Ross (2024) chapter, PRODIGI details and model comparison
finding: Idea discovery compares properties of earlier moves (line length, angle, trajectory in the nine-dot) against how much progress each move made, learns which property variation changes progress, then tries new values. The nine-dot is solved by finding a property that widens the move set, not by a conceptual insight that lines may leave the grid. The chapter says only PRODIGI of three rival accounts (representational change, outsight) is computationally tractable. Tested on the nine-dot and the Cards problem (Cunningham and MacGregor 2008).
numbers: No new effect sizes in the chapter. The implementation has no visual module; it uses a library of properties to inspect. Limited to knowledge-lean problems.
limits: Self-report by model authors. The chapter gives a qualitative claim of close approximation to human nine-dot performance, with no figures. Rivals (Ollinger, Jones and Knoblich) say representational change drives difficulty.
agent_relevance: For an LLM agent, idea discovery is a concrete operator: log each attempt as a property vector plus its progress value, then ask which property was never varied. This is testable without a model change.

source: Jones (2003) Testing two cognitive theories of insight (pre-publication copy), JEP:LMC 29(5)
finding: Jones states that criterion failure is defined from a minimum distance to goal given the moves left, so in an unlimited-move task it is never reached. He therefore tests the theory with lookahead and impasse proxies instead. The task is a spatial car-park (Rush Hour type) puzzle, not a verbal one. Both theories get some support; representational change predicts performance better.
numbers: N = 39 psychology undergraduates, 13 per condition (Normal, Rotated, Easy practice). Practice sets had optimal solutions of 6,6,6,7 and 6,8,9,10 moves, 6 to 9 cars. Prediction tested: lookahead 3 solves more and faster than lookahead 1 or 2.
quote: For unlimited move problems, criterion failure under this description will never be reached.
limits: Small cells. Pre-publication copy, not the copy of record. Spatial task only. Unlimited move count breaks the ratio, so this is a weak test of CSP as stated.
agent_relevance: Design rule: the CSP ratio needs a resource denominator. For an agent the denominator must be an explicit budget (steps or tokens left) set by the harness. Without a budget, criterion failure cannot fire and only a counter rule remains.

source: Ollinger, Jones and Knoblich (2006) Heuristics and representational change in two-move matchstick arithmetic tasks, Advances in Cognitive Psychology 2(4)
finding: Two matchstick moves. Whether the solution move reduces or increases distance to goal (the CSP manipulation) did not change solution rates. The depth of constraint that had to be relaxed did. Giving a constraint-relaxing move as a partial solution helped far more than giving a value (greedy) move. The authors say this goes against the Chronicle 2004 hill-climbing account for this task.
numbers: N = 120 (37 male, 83 female). Value type main effect F(1,118)=1.54 ns; problem type F(1,118)=37.47 p<.001; no interaction F(1,118)=.13. Partial solution type F(1,116)=45.15 p<.001; value type x partial solution interaction F(1,116)=1.66 ns. Solution rates in two problem sets: Value-Value 48.3/48.3, Value-Hybrid 36.7/31.7, Value-Operator 31.7/40.0, Value-Tautology 3.3/11.7 percent.
quote: Our experimental manipulation did not reveal any significant influence of heuristics, going against the predictions of the Criterion for Satisfactory Progress Theory.
limits: Matchstick arithmetic is symbolic, not verbal text. Ten-minute limit. Authors note a two-move task has a larger space and that this is where heuristics could matter more. Paper read in the results and discussion sections; method details read only in part.
agent_relevance: On symbolic tasks that need a change of representation, a greedy-progress monitor alone predicts nothing. Spend the budget on forced re-representation, not on a better progress score. This leans toward the representational-change side of the S5/O4 design decision.

source: Ollinger, Jones and Knoblich (2006), move analysis
finding: Solvers did choose greedy moves: most proposed moves reduced the distance between the two sides of the equation. So hill-climbing describes move choice but does not predict which problems are hard. Move choice and difficulty come apart.
numbers: 509 valid equations from 690 note-field entries: 60.89% value moves, 22.47% hybrid, 16.64% operator. Moves by effect: reduce 435 (85.46%), neutral 45 (8.85%), increase 29 (5.69%). Chi-square reduce vs other: 162.40 (-Value) and 95.19 (+Value), both p<.001. Reduce preference higher in -Value than +Value, chi2(1)=8.55, p=.01. Number of first value moves available did not predict solving (R=.30, p=.56).
limits: Notes were self-typed ideas, not forced moves. 181 of 690 entries were invalid.
agent_relevance: A harness can log the share of agent moves that lower computed distance. A high share is expected and is not by itself a stuck sign. Difficulty must be read from the trap structure, not from greediness.

source: Ollinger, Jones and Knoblich (2006), discussion of when heuristics matter
finding: The authors give a two-stage view: representational change first, then heuristics on the new representation. They also note that with a larger problem space, space size had more impact than the goal-representation differences, so heuristics become important as the space grows (Kaplan and Simon 1990).
numbers: No new numbers. Value-Operator and Value-Hybrid did not differ before a partial solution, but operator problems became harder than hybrid after a value move was given.
limits: Discussion-section reasoning, not a tested result. Possible positive transfer from solutions shown between problems.
agent_relevance: Supports the combined account (K07): a representation fix and a progress heuristic work at different stages. For text tasks this suggests the re-representation step comes before lookahead spending. Still untested on verbal tasks.

source: Europe PMC citation list for Chronicle, MacGregor and Ormerod (2004), PMID 14736293
finding: A scan of the 30 citing records indexed in Europe PMC found no study that repeats the six-coin or ten-coin first-, second- and third-move statistics. Closest items are applications and extensions (hint and verbalization studies, motor activity in the nine-dot, Katona five-square search, Act first think later on inferential planning). OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar citation APIs were rate-limited, so coverage is partial.
numbers: hitCount = 30 citing records in Europe PMC (many unrelated, for example a gene-polymorphism paper and spider-predator papers).
limits: Europe PMC indexes only part of psychology. Absence in this list is weak evidence of no replication. Titles only; abstracts of the closest items were not read.
agent_relevance: Treat the Chronicle 2004 move statistics (cell N = 19) as unreplicated. Do not tune the agent greedy-move threshold to them.

source: Ormerod, Chronicle and MacGregor (2002) Dynamics and constraints in insight problem solving, JEP:LMC 28(4) (Lancaster eprint record)
finding: Eight-coin problem, two experiments. Early strategic moves that look like progress but guarantee failure lower solution rates when available (Experiment 1). Not using visual hints about the correct first move goes with making those moves (Experiment 2). The authors say insight needs a dynamic that steers search toward the constraints, beyond wrong constraints.
numbers: No figures on the record page.
limits: Abstract only; full text not available from the repository. Numbers for this paper come from earlier evidence lines, not from this read.
agent_relevance: Same group as Chronicle 2004, so the trap-lowers-solving result has at least two papers from one lab. Still one research group.

source: David (2025) Temporal Predictors of Outcome in Reasoning Language Models
finding: A linear probe on hidden states of the last four reasoning tokens predicts final correctness from very short prefixes. Entropy plus length baselines are far weaker. The apparent drop in probe accuracy at long prefixes is a selection effect (only hard items stay long), not a loss of signal.
numbers: Qwen3-8B and Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, MATH, 750 easy (levels 1-2) + 750 hard (levels 4-5) problems; 1,500 prefixes at 4 tokens, 566 at 512. Qwen3-8B solves 85.1% easy, 32.1% hard. At 4 tokens AUC 0.84, accuracy 0.76; AUC 0.77 easy vs 0.72 hard at 4 tokens, 0.84 vs 0.76 at 32. Best entropy+length baseline AUC 0.59 at 8 tokens (0.21 below probe), gap 0.39 at 32 tokens. Greedy decoding, 512 max new tokens.
limits: One dataset (math), two 8B models, final layer only, per-prefix probes fit within distribution, possible leakage cues. The probe predicts difficulty of the item as much as progress. Needs open weights.
agent_relevance: A usable early signal exists in the model, but only through hidden states, not through text or logits. With an API-only agent it is unavailable. Do not read it as step-level progress: it is mostly item difficulty plus commitment.

source: Xu, Yu, Meng and Zhou (2026) How Far Ahead Do LLMs Plan? Uncovering the Latent Horizon in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning (Tele-Lens)
finding: Probing hidden states along the chain of thought shows a myopic horizon. On compositional tasks (parity, cycle, subset sum) the final answer is planned only about one step before the reasoning ends. Early hidden states do not predict the total reasoning length. A few pivot positions carry most of the uncertainty signal of the path.
numbers: Qwen3 8B and 32B. Top-k pivot selection gave up to 9% absolute improvement over the best baseline; best at k = 5. Qwen3-32B average AUROC over 8 tasks: perplexity 0.72 to 0.78 with 100 pivots; entropy 0.72 to 0.75; self-certainty 0.65 to 0.70 (CoT length over 7K tokens).
limits: Open-weight models, probes trained on the model's own hidden states. Does not test insight problems. Pivot gains vary by task (MATH entropy fell from 0.92 to 0.70 with pivots).
agent_relevance: A model does not hold a global plan that the harness can query. Progress toward a trap-prone goal has to be computed from task state outside the model. This supports computing the CSP ratio in the harness.

source: Kang, Deng, Xiao, Mo, Lee and Bing (2025) First Try Matters: Revisiting the Role of Reflection in Reasoning Models
finding: In eight reasoning models on five math sets, reflections after the first candidate answer are mostly confirmatory and rarely change a wrong answer into a right one. Final accuracy tracks first-answer correctness. SFT on reflection-rich rollouts mainly lifts first-answer correctness. Truncating reflection after a candidate answer saves tokens at small accuracy cost.
numbers: Over 90% of reflections are confirmatory (right to right, wrong to wrong). Corrective wrong-to-right reflections mostly under 2%. Reflections use 16.8% to 47.8% of tokens and add 1.4 to 3.5 points of accuracy. Early stopping saves 24.5% of reasoning tokens with up to 2.9% accuracy drop. Models include DeepSeek-R1-0528 and gpt-oss-20b plus 7B and 8B distills; sets AIME24, AIME25, AMC, OlympiadBench, Math500.
limits: Math only. No closed frontier model (GPT-5 class, Claude, Gemini) tested. Reflection here means after a first answer, not mid-search revision.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 is partly informed: spontaneous revision does not help much in open reasoning models up to 671B size. It is still not shown for closed frontier models or non-math tasks. Supports forced, state-triggered revision over waiting.

source: Cognitive Companion authors (2026) The cognitive companion: a lightweight parallel monitoring architecture for detecting and recovering from reasoning degradation
finding: Two parallel monitors on a small model: an LLM call every 2 steps judging the last three steps (ON_TRACK, LOOPING, DRIFTING, STUCK), and a hidden-state logistic probe fired at probability 0.55. The paper calls itself a feasibility study. No ablation of thresholds, window, or check interval; no false-positive rate; STUCK is never scored alone.
numbers: Gemma 4 E4B, 6 tasks, 6 steps, 3 runs per condition. LLM Companion cut repetition on the Liar Paradox from Jaccard 0.367 to 0.176 (-52%); overhead about 10 to 11%. Probe layer 28 CV AUROC 0.840 on 35 examples (10 degraded, 25 on track); probe overhead 0%. Mean score effect d: LLM +0.047 (SD 0.658), probe +0.471 (SD 0.893). On Qwen 1.5B and Llama 1B: 0 of 6 tasks improved.
limits: Tiny samples, labels made by the LLM Companion itself, scores judged by the same model family, no significance tests, tasks are open-ended essays not puzzles. Interventions are silent whispers, not forced changes.
agent_relevance: The only monitor design found that is run against a plain baseline, and its evidence is thin. It does not answer whether criterion failure beats a counter or entropy trigger. Gap 2 stays open.

source: CAST authors (2026) CAST: Game Solvers as Turn-Level Teachers for LLM Agents
finding: Rush Hour (6x6, 7 vehicles) as a symbolic text game. The per-action teaching signal is the drop in exact minimum remaining moves (cost-to-go) from a reverse-BFS table; no-progress moves score 0 and harmful moves negative. This is a harness-computed distance signal. The paper does not analyse greedy traps or lookahead.
numbers: Avg@4 success, in-domain / unseen difficulty (9 vehicles): Qwen3-4B-Instruct ReAct 1.1 / 0.5; GRPO 53.8 / 26.7; GiGPO 51.9 / 31.3; CAST 64.7 / 39.5. Closed models: Gemini 2.5 Pro 92.0 / 88.9; Opus 4.6 92.6 / 85.3. A learned DQN value network matched the exact solver closely, slightly lower.
limits: Training paper, not a monitoring study; reading of the first 100,000 characters only. Boards are filtered by solver-confirmed optimal length. Success is not split by trap type.
agent_relevance: Two uses. First, frontier models already solve symbolic 6x6 Rush Hour at about 92% in text, so the trap is mainly a small-model problem on this puzzle; test traps need harder boards. Second, a distance-to-goal delta from an exact or learned table is a workable per-step progress signal.

source: MentisOculi authors (2026) MentisOculi: Revealing the Limits of Reasoning with Mental Imagery
finding: Rush Hour given as an image and as a text transcription. In image form only Gemini 3 beats chance beyond Level 1. With a text transcription Gemini 3 and GPT-5.1 match humans, so the gap is visual handling, not planning. Sub-chance results are blamed on early termination and under-use of the action budget; Gemini 3 does not raise token use from Level 3 to 5 while humans spend more time.
numbers: Five levels; 200 samples per level for fine-tuned latent models (Mirage Level 1 to 5: 100.0, 96.7, 50.0, 26.7, 10.0 percent). Humans: five PhD students, 30 s limit, above 60% at Level 5. Models queried up to 3 times.
limits: Numbers per frontier model are in figures that were not in the extracted text. Humans were 5 people, two of them authors. No analysis of greedy moves or backtracking.
agent_relevance: The observed failure is stopping too early with budget unused, not falling into a greedy trap. For our design, a budget-aware progress check (distance left versus budget left) addresses under-use directly. Evidence for greedy traps in LLMs is still missing.

source: OpenRouter agent SDK docs: doom loop detection
finding: A vendor ladder for repeated identical tool calls: observe at 2, block at 3, stop at 6. Off by default. Text repeats example uses minRepeats 4. A repeat counts only when the model saw the result and retried the same call; calls with other tools in between do not reset the streak; changing inputs does.
numbers: Ladder 2/3/6. Other example values (escalate 3, block 5, stop 8) are examples, not defaults.
limits: The doc states no data or rationale for the numbers. Not an ablation.
agent_relevance: Hand-chosen thresholds of 3 and 6 match our current 3 to 6 range, but nothing here shows they are optimal or task-dependent. Gap 7 stays open; log false-positive rate per task before fixing numbers.

source: DeepEval agent loop detection metric docs
finding: Defaults: repetition_threshold 3 (score 0.5 at 3 identical calls, 0.0 at 6), similarity_threshold 0.85 for reasoning stagnation (0.0 above 0.95), call-graph cycles score 0 on a repeat on the same path. Weighted 0.40 / 0.35 / 0.25. Justification is production experience; the page's own worked example is internally inconsistent.
limits: No empirical validation. Contributor design rationale: deterministic, zero cost, zero latency.
agent_relevance: Gives a cheap baseline detector with a similarity cut that can be copied as the counter-based arm in a trigger comparison.

source: OneUptime (2026) Detect tool-call loops, dead ends and repeated agent actions in production
finding: Example guard: repeat_limit 3 on the same tool and argument fingerprint without a progress change, action_limit 20. It argues progress must be an external marker (completed task count, plan revision, changed task state) and warns that a marker changing every step defeats the detector, while one too coarse blocks real work. It tells readers to measure false positives and cost on reviewed examples.
agent_relevance: Supports defining the progress signal from task state (the CSP ratio) rather than from agent text, and tuning thresholds against a measured false-positive rate.

source: Gap search record: LLM studies on nine-dot, coin, matchstick, goal inference and lookahead budgets
finding: Searches (WebSearch until its budget ran out, then arXiv API queries) found no study that gives an LLM the nine-dot, coin or matchstick problems with a progress measure, none that tests an explicit lookahead budget against greedy traps, and none that tests goal inference from an abstract goal statement or goal examples. Nearest items: Rush Hour benchmarks (d13, d14), Tower of Hanoi budget debates, situation-puzzle studies.
numbers: Zero direct hits across about 12 targeted queries.
limits: Absence after a limited search. The WebSearch quota was used up before the goal-inference and 2002 Ormerod queries could be run. Not proof of no study.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 5 and 6 stay open and must be answered by running our own tests. Proposed first runs: six-coin and ten-coin text puzzles, a Rush Hour variant with a known trap, a goal-example arm.
